The phrase 'before 1975' signals that we are talking about an action completed prior to a specific time in the past. In English, the past perfect tense (had + past participle) is used to show that one action happened before another in the past.

  • have gone (verb (present perfect)): Present perfect tense, used for actions that happened at an unspecified time before now.

  • have (verb (present simple)): Simple present tense. Not suitable for future events, especially with a specific time reference.
  • shall have (modal verb + base verb): 'Shall' is an old-fashioned or formal way to express the future, mainly used with 'I' or 'we', but 'shall have' is not commonly used in modern English for scheduled events.
  • will have had (modal verb + perfect infinitive): Future perfect tense. Used to express that something will be completed before a certain time in the future. Not suitable here because the sentence is about the event happening, not being completed before another event.
  • will be having (modal verb + be + present participle): Future continuous tense. Used to describe an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future. This fits the context of a scheduled examination next month.
Related structure or vocabulary: Future continuous tense (will be + V-ing): Used to talk about actions that will be happening at a specific time in the future.

The blank in the sentence 'Look at those black clouds! It________' requires a verb form that expresses a prediction based on present evidence. In English, when we make a prediction about the near future based on something we can see or evidence in the present (like seeing black clouds), we use 'be going to' + verb. Therefore, the correct answer is 'is going to rain.'
  • is going to rain (future expression): This is the correct form to express a prediction based on present evidence. 'Be going to' + verb is used when we see signs that something will happen soon.
  • will rain (future expression): 'Will' is used for predictions not based on present evidence, or for decisions made at the moment of speaking. Here, we have evidence (black clouds), so 'will' is not the best choice.
  • would rain (modal verb (past/future in the past)): 'Would' is the past tense of 'will' or used in conditional sentences. It is not suitable for this context.
  • can rain (modal verb (ability/possibility)): 'Can' expresses ability or possibility in general, not a prediction based on evidence. It is not correct here.
Related structure or vocabulary: be going to + verb: used for predictions based on present evidence; will + verb: used for spontaneous decisions or predictions without present evidence
